questions.stem: What provides the pressure needed for ultrafiltration in the glomerulus?

options.text: The difference in diameter between the afferent and efferent arterioles
Osmotic pressure from proteins in the filtrate
The contraction of smooth muscle in the nephron

questions.explanation: High blood pressure in the glomerulus is created because the afferent arteriole (bringing blood in) is wider than the efferent arteriole (taking blood out). This pressure difference forces small molecules through the filtration barrier.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT found in the glomerular filtrate?
questions.explanation: Proteins and blood cells are too large to pass through the filtration barrier (basement membrane and podocytes) during ultrafiltration. Small molecules like water, glucose, urea, and salts pass through into the Bowman's capsule.

questions.stem: Approximately how much filtrate do the kidneys produce each day?
questions.explanation: The kidneys filter approximately 180 litres of blood plasma each day. However, most of this is reabsorbed, so only about 1-2 litres of urine is actually produced daily.

questions.stem: What is the name of the cup-shaped structure that collects the filtrate from the glomerulus?
questions.explanation: Bowman's capsule is the cup-shaped structure that surrounds the glomerulus and collects the filtrate produced during ultrafiltration. The filtrate then passes into the proximal convoluted tubule.

questions.stem: Which cells form part of the filtration barrier in the glomerulus, wrapping around the capillaries with finger-like projections?
questions.explanation: Podocytes are specialised cells that wrap around the glomerular capillaries with finger-like projections. They form part of the filtration barrier, with gaps between projections allowing small molecules to pass through while retaining large molecules.

questions.stem: Why is ultrafiltration described as a non-selective process?

options.text: Because it filters all small molecules regardless of whether they are useful or waste
Because it only filters waste products from the blood
Because it uses active transport to move molecules
Because it does not require any energy

questions.explanation: Ultrafiltration is non-selective because all small molecules (including useful ones like glucose and amino acids) are forced through the filtration barrier by pressure, along with waste products like urea. Useful substances must then be reabsorbed later.

questions.stem: What would happen to the rate of ultrafiltration if a person's blood pressure dropped significantly?

options.text: It would stay the same because the kidneys regulate their own pressure
It would increase because less blood enters the kidney
It would increase because the efferent arteriole would widen
It would decrease because there is less pressure to force molecules through the filter

questions.explanation: Ultrafiltration relies on high blood pressure in the glomerulus to force small molecules through the filtration barrier. If blood pressure drops, there is less force driving filtration, so the rate of ultrafiltration would decrease.
